section_summary: This section centers on American and Allied efforts to understand or restrict Japan’s access to strategic materials in mid-1941. It includes an analysis of Japan’s dependence on imported iron and steel inputs; extensive public and congressional protests over petroleum and other war-material exports; reports of Japanese attempts to buy copper, chrome, tungsten, lead, and other minerals; and confidential reporting on Japanese–Netherlands East Indies rubber negotiations. The records also document State Department explanations of export licensing and petroleum-market data showing continued shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: The Supply Position in the Iron and Steel Industry in Japan
subfiles.from: John K. Davis, Department of State
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s iron and steel production and its dependence on imported ore, pig iron, and scrap.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes a British Embassy study showing that Japanese steel output had increased but remained dependent on imported raw materials, especially American scrap and ore from Malaya and the Philippines. It evaluates the effect of partial and complete embargoes and argues that reducing Malayan, Philippine, Indian, and American supplies would materially constrain Japanese war production. It also discusses using restrictions on manganese, chrome, tungsten, and other alloys to impair steel quality.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 849 on Kokumin Commentary About American Oil Restrictions
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese newspaper criticism of reported American restrictions on oil shipments from the eastern United States.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 849: Kokumin calls American oil restrictions unsurprising and hysterical, says oil should be moved from elsewhere if the eastern shortage is real, and urges caution.

subfiles.title: Barry Transmittal of McGrath Letter
subfiles.from: William B. Barry, House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s complaint about oil exports and asks the Department to respond.
subfiles.summary: Representative Barry submits a constituent's communication, asking that its request be met and the letter returned with the reply.

subfiles.title: McGrath Protest Against Oil Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: John M. McGrath
subfiles.about: Asks why Americans face restrictions on domestic oil use while Japan continues to receive supplies.
subfiles.summary: McGrath cites a June 13 Herald Tribune report that oil shipments to Japan might stop, and objects that Americans are restrained while an enemy is supplied.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to William B. Barry
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Barry’s referral of John M. McGrath’s letter concerning oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Department acknowledges Barry's June 20 communication and McGrath's letter for prompt attention.

subfiles.title: Reply to Barry on Petroleum Export Controls
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains petroleum export licensing and distinguishes overseas exports from the eastern domestic transportation shortage.
subfiles.summary: Welles says most petroleum needed licenses, extended to all products June 20; licenses are reviewed for defense; eastern gasoline curtailment arises from transport problems, while Japan-bound shipments leave the Pacific Coast in foreign vessels.

subfiles.title: Letter to Clayton Concerning Japanese Purchases of Peruvian Lead
subfiles.from: Thomas K. Finletter
subfiles.about: Forwards a paraphrased telegram about a reported Japanese effort to acquire Peruvian lead production and supplies.
subfiles.summary: Finletter encloses a Lima message on reports that Japan seeks all Peruvian lead; the embassy should determine whether the US can acquire it.

subfiles.title: Ickes Transmittal of Petroleum-Export Protests
subfiles.from: Harold L. Ickes, Petroleum Coordinator for National Defense
subfiles.about: Forwards protests against petroleum exports to Japan because petroleum export policy falls under State Department jurisdiction.
subfiles.summary: Ickes sends protests against petroleum shipments to Japan, noting his office told writers State controls export policy.

subfiles.title: List of Senders Protesting Petroleum Exports
subfiles.from: Office of the Petroleum Coordinator for National Defense
subfiles.about: Lists organizations and individuals whose protests accompanied Ickes’s June 21 transmittal.
subfiles.summary: The five-page attachment names individuals and civic, religious, and political groups from across the United States and abroad that protested petroleum exports to Japan. It documents the breadth and geographic distribution of public opposition to supplying Japan with oil.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Protest Against Exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Linne Gal, signature uncertain
subfiles.to: Petroleum Coordinator or Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Objects to sending petroleum, iron, and scrap to Japan while Americans face shortages and higher prices.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten, degraded protest against strategic exports to Japan, saying foreign buyers pay high prices while domestic supplies grow scarce.

subfiles.title: The Customer Across the Pacific
subfiles.about: Satirizes the prospect of American gasoline and oil rationing while Japan remains a customer.
subfiles.summary: Cartoon 'The Customer Across the Pacific' contrasts gasless Sundays and rationing in America with continued exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Chandler Transmittal of Richmond Letter
subfiles.from: Albert B. Chandler, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter from Murray State Teachers College president James H. Richmond.
subfiles.summary: Senator Chandler sends Richmond's letter on public concern over oil and gasoline sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Richmond Letter Opposing Oil and Gasoline Sales to Japan
subfiles.from: James H. Richmond
subfiles.about: Questions why the United States continues selling oil and gasoline to Japan and asks for a public explanation.
subfiles.summary: Richmond grants the administration may have confidential information but says the policy looks dangerous; fears oil may reach Germany or be stored against the US; urges halting sales or explaining them.

subfiles.title: Reply to Chandler on Petroleum Export Licensing
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the petroleum export-license system in response to James H. Richmond’s protest.
subfiles.summary: Welles states that most petroleum exports had long required licenses and that all petroleum products came under licensing on June 20. Applications were considered individually, with no license granted when its effects were judged detrimental to national defense. He adds that controls were continually adjusted and returns Richmond’s letter.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Chandler
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Chandler’s letter forwarding James H. Richmond’s protest.
subfiles.summary: Department acknowledges Chandler's June 23 letter and Richmond's communication for prompt attention.

subfiles.title: Gamble Transmittal of Pleasantville Protest Telegram
subfiles.from: Ralph A. Gamble, House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Forwards a telegram from three Pleasantville women protesting oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gamble sends a telegram from three Pleasantville women and asks information for a reply.

subfiles.title: Pleasantville Telegram Protesting Oil Shipments
subfiles.from: Mrs. J. W. Frost, Mrs. Arthur O. Choate, and Mrs. Allen Coggeshall
subfiles.about: Protests sending oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Degraded telegram from three Pleasantville, New York women protesting oil to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Gamble on Petroleum Export Controls
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains petroleum export licensing in response to the Pleasantville protest telegram.
subfiles.summary: Welles explains that most petroleum exports required licenses and that licensing was extended to all petroleum products on June 20. Applications were evaluated against national-defense considerations, and policy remained subject to continuing adjustment. The protest telegram is returned.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Gamble
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Gamble’s letter and the Pleasantville protest telegram.
subfiles.summary: Department acknowledges the June 23 referral from Gamble on oil to Japan.

subfiles.title: Senate Referral of Amy Wade Communication
subfiles.from: Office of Senator Tom Connally
subfiles.about: Refers Amy Wade’s communication for consideration and a report.
subfiles.summary: Senate referral form asking favorable consideration of Amy Wade's communication and a report.

subfiles.title: Amy Wade Letter on Sales of War Materials
subfiles.from: Amy Wade
subfiles.about: Asks why American firms continue selling war materials to Japan, Germany, and intermediaries while citizens bear defense and relief costs.
subfiles.summary: Wade, a Texas civic woman, describes confusion over policy, argues private firms profit supplying threatening countries while the public pays, and asks Connally for an explanation to share.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Connally Regarding Amy Wade
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Connally’s referral of Amy Wade’s letter on war-material sales.
subfiles.summary: Department acknowledges Connally's communication and Amy Wade's letter for prompt attention.

subfiles.title: Reply to Connally on Export-Control Authority
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory and administrative framework governing exports of military equipment and strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: Welles cites section 6 of the July 2, 1940 act, names General Maxwell as Export Administrator, says State issues licenses under his directives, rules are continually revised, and Wade's concerns are under consideration.

subfiles.title: Weston Letter Transmitting Youth Conference Resolutions
subfiles.from: Hugh W. Weston, Mid-West Conference of the Young People's Religious Union
subfiles.about: Transmits conference resolutions, including a petition for an embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Weston reports Lake Geneva conference votes June 15-22: 36 for and none against an embargo of war materials to Japan, 10 abstaining; other resolutions on conscripts, labor and academic freedom.

subfiles.title: Petition Favoring an Embargo of War Materials to Japan and Signatures
subfiles.from: Members of the Mid-West Conference of the Young People's Religious Union and other signatories
subfiles.to: United States Government and local church groups
subfiles.about: Calls for the immediate termination of shipments to Japan of war materials and raw materials essential to war production.
subfiles.summary: Petition for an embargo on war materials to Japan, citing rising oil and gasoline shipments and cotton, copper and scrap; rejects appeasement by trade; many signatures.

subfiles.title: Lake Geneva Assembly Resolutions
subfiles.from: Mid-West Conference of the Young People's Religious Union
subfiles.to: United States Government and local church groups
subfiles.about: Presents resolutions on a Japan embargo, anti-discrimination legislation, academic freedom, labor rights, conscript welfare, and opposition to conscripting women.
subfiles.summary: Lake Geneva resolutions demand halting war-material shipments to Japan and back anti-poll-tax and anti-discrimination measures, the American Youth Act, academic freedom, labor rights and limits on war profits.

subfiles.title: Overseas Trading Corporation Inquiry on Chrome and Tungsten Sales
subfiles.from: William I. Vidor, Overseas Trading Corporation
subfiles.about: Asks whether the company should quote Mitsui on Philippine chrome ore and Peruvian tungsten ore.
subfiles.summary: Vidor says Mitsui asked quotations for Philippine chrome ore and Peruvian tungsten ore; he seeks guidance on US policy before quoting.

subfiles.title: Reply to Vidor on Chrome and Tungsten
subfiles.from: Thomas K. Finletter, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Advises that the Federal Loan Agency is interested in buying the chrome and tungsten offered to Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: Finletter says the Federal Loan Agency is interested in the Philippine chrome and Peruvian tungsten ores and invites Vidor to Washington.

subfiles.title: Davies Transmittal of Additional Petroleum-Export Protests
subfiles.from: R. K. Davies, Deputy Petroleum Coordinator
subfiles.about: Forwards another group of protests against petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Davies encloses a list of correspondents protesting petroleum exports, again noting authority rests with State, not Interior.

subfiles.title: List of Additional Petroleum-Export Protesters
subfiles.from: Office of the Deputy Petroleum Coordinator for National Defense
subfiles.about: Lists eighty-two senders of communications protesting petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The attachment records senators, aid-to-China advocates, and private citizens from across the United States who objected to petroleum shipments to Japan. Several correspondents had also appeared in earlier congressional referrals, including the three Pleasantville women.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Ickes and Davies
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of 224 protests forwarded by Ickes and eighty-two more forwarded by Davies.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges Ickes's June 21 package of 224 communications and Davies's June 27 letter with eighty-two more against petroleum exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hayden Transmittal of Second McGinley Letter
subfiles.from: Carl Hayden, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Forwards another letter from H. F. McGinley and asks for further comment on oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hayden encloses McGinley's second complaint and asks for information to reply.

subfiles.title: McGinley Critique of the Petroleum Licensing System
subfiles.from: H. F. McGinley
subfiles.about: Argues that petroleum licensing is ineffective because oil continues to reach Japan.
subfiles.summary: McGinley calls the earlier explanation evasive, asks why licensing is not used to stop supplies to a likely enemy, and contrasts exports with billions spent on defense.

subfiles.title: Reply to Hayden Regarding McGinley
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Declines to disclose the specific considerations behind individual petroleum-export licenses.
subfiles.summary: Welles regrets McGinley's dissatisfaction but cannot disclose license factors; all petroleum exports needed licenses after June 20, weighing production, consumption, defense and foreign relations; letter returned.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Hayden
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Hayden’s second McGinley communication.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms receipt of the senator’s enclosure from his Kingman constituent. It promises prompt consideration.

subfiles.title: Wilson-Martin Protest Against Loading the Azuma Maru
subfiles.from: Edward Jobbins, Wilson-Martin Division
subfiles.about: Protests the loading of oil aboard the Japanese ship Azuma Maru in Philadelphia while a defense-related factory lacks fuel.
subfiles.summary: Jobbins protests the Azuma Maru loading oil at Philadelphia's Pier 98 while his defense-related plant struggles for fuel oil and gasoline.

subfiles.title: Jobbins Telegram to Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Edward Jobbins
subfiles.about: Strongly protests loading oil onto the Japanese transport Azuma Maru at Philadelphia.
subfiles.summary: Jobbins telegraphs Roosevelt that Wilson-Martin, a defense unit, faces fuel shortages that could force a shutdown.

subfiles.title: Senate Referral of Parrett Communication
subfiles.from: Office of Senator Tom Connally
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent communication and clipping for consideration and report.
subfiles.summary: Senate referral form forwarding Mrs. F. J. Parrett's material for favorable consideration and a report.

subfiles.title: Clipping on Petroleum and Tin Exports
subfiles.from: Waco News-Tribune
subfiles.about: Reports figures for American petroleum exports to Japan and tin exports to Portugal.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: American firms shipped over 53.5 million gallons of petroleum products to Japan in early 1941, and large tin exports to Portugal may be diverted to Germany.

subfiles.title: Reply to Connally Regarding Parrett’s Clipping
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains export-control law and administration in response to Parrett’s clipping about strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: Welles cites the July 2, 1940 statute, explains the roles of the Export Administrator and State, and says the Waco News-Tribune clipping issues are under careful attention.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1593 on Chilean Blister Copper for Japan
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, Santiago
subfiles.about: Reports that a New York corporation allegedly released 1,600 tons of Chilean blister copper for sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 1593: International Minerals and Metals, holding the M'Zaita copper contract, reportedly let the Chilean firm sell 1,600 tons of blister copper to Japan in 1941; Bowers suggests US agencies discuss it with the company.

subfiles.title: Invitation to International Minerals and Metals Corporation
subfiles.from: Thomas K. Finletter
subfiles.about: Requests a Washington meeting concerning the corporation’s contract for Chilean blister copper.
subfiles.summary: Finletter asks an International Minerals and Metals representative to visit Washington about its M'Zaita blister-copper contract.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Report on Peruvian Strategic-Material Shipments
subfiles.from: Naval Attaché, Peru
subfiles.about: Points to a report on April 1941 shipments of cotton and strategic materials from Peru to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Naval Attaché Report 162-41 on Peruvian cotton and strategic-material shipments to Japan in April 1941 (894.20223/79).

subfiles.title: Routing Memorandum on Mexican Strategic-Material Correspondence
subfiles.from: Department of State official, initials D.M.S.
subfiles.about: States that instructions should ensure correspondence about strategic materials in Mexico is routed to the proper office.
subfiles.summary: Memo says the writer examined the matter and expects new instructions to route Mexican strategic-material correspondence promptly.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese Requests for Strategic Materials in Mexico
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese approach to Banco Nacional de México seeking numerous metals and minerals.
subfiles.summary: A bank official told the Commercial Attaché that Japanese interests wanted monthly quantities of lead, zinc, molybdenum, tungsten, and black mica, as well as all available vanadium, platinum, osmium, radium, and tin-plate scrap. The bank official provided the information so the Department would know Japanese demand for Mexican strategic materials.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Suppress Published Japan Shipment Data
subfiles.from: Rush M. Blodget, Oil Producers Agency of California
subfiles.to: Compiler of the California Weekly Petroleum Bulletin
subfiles.about: Orders the bulletin to omit data from which petroleum shipments to Japan could be determined.
subfiles.summary: Blodget orders the bulletin staff to stop publishing direct or inferable Japan shipment figures; data still collected privately, released only to federal officials or with Vander Leck's authorization.

subfiles.title: California Weekly Petroleum Bulletin No. 1941-25
subfiles.from: Oil Producers Agency of California
subfiles.about: Reports California petroleum production, refining, exports, and stock changes for the week ended June 21, including exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: California bulletin: exports to Japan fell to 40,800 barrels a day for the week, averaging 48,400 in June; discusses lost tanker markets, possible aid to Russia and inventories.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5653
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes confidential information on Japanese–Netherlands East Indies negotiations, especially rubber supplies.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Tokyo despatch 5653: British-Dutch cooperation; Japan claims 96,950 tons annual rubber needs and seeks 30,000 from the Indies, Dutch offering 15,000; American scrap rubber exports to Japan rose.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5653: Exports from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports confidential discussions concerning Japan’s demands for rubber from the Netherlands East Indies and related trade negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Embassy officers relayed W. H. de Roos’s account of Japanese diplomatic pressure on British and Dutch representatives to secure a successful outcome at Batavia. Japanese officials claimed annual rubber needs of 96,950 tons, sought roughly 30,000 tons from the Netherlands East Indies, and portrayed domestic shortages as acute, while promising that Indies rubber would not be re-exported to Germany. The Dutch challenged Japan’s figures and noted that continued, increasing American scrap-rubber exports contradicted Japanese assertions that this source had ended. The despatch continues beyond page 240.
